The global equity tape is remarkably resilient given the weight of the negative weekend news flow.

The geopolitical situation is genuinely deteriorating with Iran tightening its grip on global energy supply via Hormuz, aligned militias in Iraq, and the Houthis, while Russian refining capacity continues to be taken offline. Today's diplomatic optimism could easily prove to be wishful thinking, and the recent energy price spike has not yet fully worked its way through corporate earnings and consumer spending.

tts_summary:
Good morning. Here's your morning briefing for Monday, September 21st.

Futures are rallying despite a genuinely ugly weekend news cycle. S&P futures are up about 49 points or 65 basis points. Nasdaq is up 110 basis points. Small caps are up 47 basis points. Asia closed broadly higher — Hong Kong up over 1 percent, Korea up 1.65 percent. Europe is up 85 to 120 basis points. The rally is confounding because almost every major headline from the weekend was negative, but markets are trading on one specific hope: diplomatic progress at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, which runs all week.

Trump was apparently on the verge of greenlighting air strikes against the Houthis Sunday night before backing off at the last minute, and then said he'd be open to meeting Iran's president at the General Assembly. That's the trade right now. Markets believe that even a small improvement in Middle East tensions could trigger a sharp drop in oil — Brent is already sliding 170 basis points to around $102 a barrel — and if oil were to sustainably drop, you'd get a cascade of bullish effects: lower yields, less hawkish monetary policy, better margins, improved consumer confidence.

On rates, Treasuries have a bid this morning with yields down 2 to 3 basis points across the curve. But the Fed is still in hawkish mode. Markets are pricing roughly 33 basis points of additional rate hikes over the final two meetings of the year, with about 50/50 odds of a move at the October 28th meeting. Kansas City Fed's Schmid and Minneapolis Fed's Kashkari both warned over the weekend that inflation is running hot across the entire economy, not just in energy. Separately, Treasury plans to flood the market with over one trillion dollars in T-bills over the next 12 months, pushing short-term debt well above its own target threshold.

On the company side, Oracle is facing fresh scrutiny after an FT report this weekend revealed that efforts to offload debt tied to its massive New Mexico data center — internally called Project Jupiter — have hit a wall. That comes alongside a string of other AI infrastructure concerns: Anthropic's IPO has been delayed, its 2027 revenue projections disappointed, and OpenAI is projecting roughly 280 billion dollars in negative free cash flow between now and 2030. Nscale, a London-based cloud firm, filed its S1 Friday and plans to list on the New York Stock Exchange. Despite all this, data center pick-and-shovel names are outperforming in Europe this morning.

On the positive side, Disney's parks business is holding up well, outperforming peers through price promotions and package deals. Novo Nordisk is slumping in Europe after disappointing investors at its analyst day by failing to provide specific financial targets. And Paramount is in advanced talks with California's attorney general to settle the lawsuit blocking its Warner merger, potentially agreeing to preserve CNN's editorial independence and divest Comedy Central.

The Trump-Xi summit is set for Thursday, and modest tariff reductions on around 30 billion dollars worth of goods could be announced, along with possible elimination of Chinese tariffs on American LNG. Don't expect a major breakthrough on the broader trade truce extension — Washington is still expected to push aggregate China tariffs back toward pre-court ruling levels in the coming weeks.

Bottom line: today is all about geopolitical optionality. The news is objectively bad, but markets are buying the idea that things are so bad they can only get better. Watch for any headline out of the General Assembly. If Iran signals openness to talks, oil could drop fast and this rally has legs. If the diplomacy stalls, reality will reassert itself quickly.
